entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Kidinnu, a distinguished Chaldean astronomer and mathematician active in Babylon during the late Achaemenid and early Hellenistic periods, around 379-368 BCE, was instrumental in refining Babylonian astronomical observations and developing sophisticated mathematical models for predicting celestial phenomena. His work laid foundational elements for Hellenistic astronomy, particularly influencing Hipparchus and Ptolemy, and exemplified the advanced scientific traditions of Mesopotamia before its decline. Known to Greek and Roman writers as Kidenas (Strabo), Cidenas (Pliny the Elder), and Kidynas (Vettius Valens), his contributions mark a pinnacle of pre-Greek observational and computational astronomy.

Kidinnu's primary contribution was the precise determination of astronomical constants, including the length of the synodic month (29 days, 12 hours, 44 minutes, 3.3 seconds) and the tropical year, which was remarkably accurate for his time. He is widely credited with developing or refining System B of Babylonian astronomy, a sophisticated mathematical scheme that employed zigzag functions to describe the variable speed of the moon and planets. This intricate system allowed for highly accurate predictions of eclipses and planetary positions, as evidenced in ephemerides and almanacs from the Seleucid era, demonstrating a profound understanding of celestial mechanics and periodicity.
